in_context.text: This verse continues a rule for which widows the church should put on its list for support. Verse 9 says such a widow must be at least sixty and have been the wife of one man. Verse 10 adds that she must have a good name for a life of good works, such as raising children, hosting strangers, washing believers' feet, and helping the suffering.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle writes the letter, naming himself at the start. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote it in his name.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: Older widows who might be "taken into the number" of widows the church supports. Younger widows are handled differently in the verses that follow.

what.text: The verse lists the record of service that should mark a widow the church takes on. She should already be known for caring for others: children, strangers, fellow believers, and people in trouble. The list ends by summing her up as one who has "diligently followed every good work."

events.text: The instructions address the ongoing life of the Ephesian church, which faced false teaching from within. The text gives no specific event.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's two Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110, though others defend the earlier date.

where.text: The church at Ephesus, a wealthy port and capital of the Roman province of Asia. The letter does not say where Paul wrote from, though he may have been in Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul wants the church to support widows who are truly in need and of proven character. Families should care for their own widows, so the church can help those who are "widows indeed."

big_picture.text: The passage is part of a section on caring for groups in the church. It fits the letter's theme that belief and behavior belong together, and that leaders and those honored by the church should have proven character.

for_readers.text: The verse gives a picture of a faithful life as practical, humble service. The same call to good works and hospitality appears elsewhere in Scripture.

why_it_matters.text: The word means being borne witness to. Her good works must be known and confirmed by others, not just claimed.
It means to entertain strangers, a single Greek word for hospitality. The lexicon lists this verse as its only New Testament use.
The same verb with "feet" is used in John 13, where the lexicon cites it. Washing feet was a humble act of service, as in Luke 7:44, where Jesus notes a host who gave him no water for his feet.
This word for giving aid appears again in verse 16, where families and the church "relieve" widows. The widow who once relieved others is now the one to be relieved.
The word pictures being pressed or squeezed, and metaphorically being oppressed or distressed. It points to people under real hardship, not mild inconvenience.

takeaway.text: This verse is a church rule about supporting older widows, not a general checklist for all women. It shows that the church honored a life already spent serving others, through hospitality, humble care, and help for the suffering.

unsupported.reason: The cited verses (5:4, 5:8, 5:16) cover family responsibility and church relief for 'widows indeed.' None of them says the widows must be 'of proven character.' That requirement comes from 5:9-10, which this claim does not cite.
